pages.name: Contractor Orientation
pages.html:
GM Only

Session 0 — Contractor Orientation

A complete GM-facing run sheet for forming the party before S01 begins.

Objective. QuestRabbit should not create the party. By the end of Session 0, QuestRabbit should be hiring a contractor team that already has history, trust, friction, unfinished business and a reason to stay together.

Recommended Running Order

TimeSectionOutcome
00:00–00:10Welcome & campaign premiseEveryone understands Brandmere, QuestRabbit and the level 1–20 campaign structure.
00:10–00:25Tone & expectationsThe group agrees the balance of comedy, danger, investigation, politics and adventuring.
00:25–00:45House rules, table policy & safetyMechanical and social expectations are explicit before characters are finalised.
00:45–01:05Company positionsPlayers understand how the official Acquisitions Incorporated franchise subsystem is being used.
01:05–01:45Character creation & concept alignmentLevel 1 concepts, ability scores, backgrounds and party suitability are settled.
01:45–02:05QuestRabbit specialist positionsEach PC chooses a distinct company position where practical.
02:05–03:00Communal backstory workshopThe team creates three shared pre-campaign jobs and their consequences.
03:00–03:25Personnel filesEach PC gains motivations, flaws, obligations, secrets and usable hooks.
03:25–03:40Relationships & practical setupAt least two PC connections each; Foundry and campaign communication confirmed.
03:40–03:50Stars & WishesImmediate calibration before S01.

If time runs short: protect the communal-history workshop. Character-sheet polish and technical questions can continue after the session; the shared past is the material that makes Session 1 feel like an established team rather than six strangers standing beside the same quest giver.

Campaign Pitch

Brandmere is a city where adventuring has been franchised. You begin as low-level independent adventurers signing with QuestRabbit Adventuring Solutions, a cheerful contractor agency with glowing job boards, corporate badges and a completely reasonable thirty-percent commission. QuestRabbit sends contractors to solve the problems fantasy corporations would rather not put in writing: missing staff, magical workplace incidents, cursed products, hostile takeovers, monsters in storerooms, franchise disputes and jobs that technically never existed.

At first, Franchise Wars is bright corporate fantasy-comedy: absurd brands, bad management, dangerous jobs and heroic people trying to survive the shift. The comedy remains, but the stakes become more serious as you discover that Brandmere's corporate structure is stranger, older and more dangerous than it looks.

Core Tone

  • The satire points upward. Owners, executives, monopolies, systems and corporate absurdity are the targets. Ordinary workers are people, not punchlines.
  • Comedy does not erase consequence. Ridiculous situations can still hurt people and change the city.
  • The party has agency. They may negotiate, refuse, expose, embarrass, help or exploit employers. They do not need to admire QuestRabbit or Corporate Row.
  • The campaign premise is still binding. Every character needs a reason to take dangerous work and a reason to keep adventuring with the team.

Character Creation Baseline

  • Starting level: 1.
  • Ability scores: Standard Array or 27-point buy. No rolled ability scores.
  • Use the table's declared player-option baseline consistently. Do not combine legacy/current versions of the same feature unless approved.
  • Normal class/background starting equipment plus one small themed trinket from the character's previous life.
  • Acquisitions Incorporated company positions sit beside class/background; they do not replace either.
  • Individual written backstories may follow Session 0. Useful unfinished business matters more than length; the existing maximum remains ten pages.

Questions to Ask the Whole Table

Campaign Mix

How much do you want of roleplay, combat, investigation, exploration, politics, puzzles, business management, horror and comedy?

Group Contract

What makes this team stay together when a contract becomes inconvenient, unprofitable or morally ugly?

Character Principle

What are you willing to sell — and what are you not willing to sell?

QuestRabbit

Why are you applying now rather than remaining completely independent?

Do Not Reveal During Session 0

  • The true meaning of Rabbit Rating.
  • The metaphysical purpose of the party's signatures.
  • Creation & Company's real position in the ownership structure.
  • The Final Contract, Clause 77-B, or the true function of Receipts.
  • The hidden mechanics of the Commons Tally.
  • The later Board vote.
  • The significance of the Franchise Below.

Players only need to know that contracts, reviews, records and reputation matter in Brandmere.

Close Checklist

  • Character concept, class, species and background confirmed.
  • Ability score method completed.
  • Company position chosen for every PC; roles unique where practical.
  • Every character has a reason to take QuestRabbit work.
  • Three communal past jobs exist.
  • At least one friendly NPC, one rival/debt and one unpaid act of kindness exist.
  • Every PC has at least two relationships with other PCs.
  • Every PC has at least one unresolved personal hook.
  • Safety additions are recorded privately.
  • Foundry access and campaign communication work.
  • Stars & Wishes have been completed.
  • No PC is built around permanently refusing the campaign premise.

After Session 0

Record character names, players, class/background/species, company positions, core motivations, flaws, hard lines, corporate temptations, important NPCs, the three shared jobs, party relationships, rival/debt, communal keepsake, safety notes and the night's Stars & Wishes. These become immediate inputs for personal side contracts and recurring NPCs.

Player Handbook

Welcome, Contractor

Everything a player needs before the first shift.

You are a QuestRabbit contractor in Brandmere, the City of Franchises. Adventuring here is a gig. You pick up contracts from the glowing boards at the Warren, do the dangerous part, and QuestRabbit takes thirty per cent.

This handbook is yours to read at any time. It collects the orientation material, the house rules, the city as your characters know it, and five ready-to-play contractors if you would rather start right away.

  • @FWLink[JournalEntry|fw.player.handbook|Evidence, Favours and Leverage]{Evidence, Favours and Leverage}: three things worth keeping.
  • @FWLink[JournalEntry|fw.player.handbook|House Rules]{House Rules} and @FWLink[JournalEntry|fw.player.handbook|Table Policy & Safety]{Table Policy & Safety}.

pages.name: Brandmere for Contractors
pages.html:
Player Handbook

Brandmere for Contractors

What everyone in the city knows.

Brandmere is a harbour city of two hundred thousand people on a river delta where three trade roads meet the sea. A century ago it became the first city to grant franchise charters. Now every chain has a flagship here and every holding company a tower. The motto over the Old Gate reads Fides et Mercatura, “Trust and Trade”. Someone has added a ™.

Getting Along

  • Government: the Chamber of Commerce, a council of franchise owners weighted by market share. The Lord Mayor cuts ribbons.
  • Law: the City Watch, mostly paid in Dungeon Donuts vouchers. Disputes go to the Arbitration Court on Guild Row, where both sides pay a filing fee.
  • Money: ordinary coin, plus loyalty points, which more shops accept than gold. Points cannot be turned back into coin.
  • News: The Brandmere Crier (small, independent, brave) and The Market Herald (large, glossy, always has a twist).
  • Temples: still standing, though most rent their forecourts to kiosks.

Districts

Guild Row
Offices, courts and the Warren, QuestRabbit’s cheerful burrow-tower, where job boards glow when a contract posts. Your handler, Pip Ashworth, has a desk in the lobby beside a ficus.
Drive-Thru Row
A mile of fast-food flagships open all night: THAC0 Spell, Murder King, Wight Castle, Five Wights and more. Carts queue in the road.
Corporate Row
The towers. Every lobby has a fountain and a receptionist with a clipboard.
The Old Independents’ Quarter
Crooked streets and family shops that refuse franchise deals. The Tankard & Tallow on Tallow Lane serves the best stew in the city and asks no questions.
The Harbour & Driftwood Quarter
Docks, fish markets and sailors’ taverns. A district sank beyond the breakwater forty years ago; its rooftops show at low tide.
The Songbird Quarter
Music halls and all-night cafés. Street performers need a licence.
The Rows
Trade streets named for crafts that franchises pushed out: Adventurers’ Row, Brewer’s Row, Tinkers’ Row, Gamblers’ Row.
The Retail Park
Outside the old walls: the Wand-Mart Supercentre, Quest Buy, the CostCo-op and the IKEA Mimic showroom. Night staff don’t talk about the Showroom.
Camp Brandmere
The fortified depot of the Little Caesars Legion, which treats pizza delivery as a military occupation.
Planar Quay
A dock that isn’t on the river. Portals to other planes, leased by the hour. Customs checks your luggage and your soul.

pages.name: How the Work Works
pages.html:
Player Handbook

How the Work Works

Contracts, grades, pay and stars.

Contract Grades

GradeLevelsTypical workBase pay
Copper1–4Pest control, deliveries, missing employees25–150 gp
Silver5–8Monster nests, sabotage, workplace hauntings300–1,500 gp
Gold9–12Interplanar procurement, corporate warfare2,000–8,000 gp
Platinum13–16Demonic mergers, ancient franchises10,000–40,000 gp
Black Card17–20Jobs that technically never existedPayment in kind

The Thirty Per Cent

QuestRabbit deducts thirty per cent of every fee. Pip will tell you this is industry standard. You can try negotiating directly with a client to keep the whole fee, but work done off the board doesn’t count toward your rating.

The Rabbit Rating

Your team shares one rating, from one to five stars. It starts at one star when you sign your Contractor Agreement. Higher ratings unlock better work.

StarsUnlocks
★Copper contracts; a badge
★★Silver contracts; a QuestRabbit expense account (50 gp/month)
★★★Gold contracts
★★★★Platinum contracts; a private office at the Warren
★★★★★Black Card contracts

Stars come from finishing major jobs and from the public liking you. QuestRabbit says the rating is a customer-satisfaction score.

Levelling

Characters level up by milestone, after major contracts or an equivalent run of side work.

pages.name: Evidence, Favours and Leverage
pages.html:
Player Handbook

Evidence, Favours and Leverage

Three things worth keeping track of.

Keep the Paperwork

In Brandmere, paper is power. When the GM hands you a document, a receipt, a note or a contract, keep it. The physical card or the journal page is the thing itself: if it is lost, it is gone. Your team should appoint someone to hold the file.

Leverage

Leverage is dirt, debts, favours and secrets your team holds over a specific corporation. You usually earn 1 Leverage by finishing a contract with the truth exposed rather than buried. Spend a point against that corporation for one of these:

  • Advantage on one Charisma check against them.
  • Access: a meeting, a warehouse, a file, a private dining room.
  • Cover: their security looks the other way for one scene.

Accepting a corporation’s “bonus” can cost you Leverage against it. So can heavy-handed use.

Favours Done for Free

Keep a list of the people and groups you help without being paid, and the promises you make and keep. The GM will tell you when someone joins it. People on that list turn up when you need them: once a session you can call on one for a small favour, no roll needed.

pages.name: House Rules
pages.html:
Player Facing

House Rules

The mechanical rules used throughout Franchise Wars.

Powerful Critical Hits

On a natural 20 attack, deal the maximum value of the attack's normal damage dice, then roll those damage dice normally and add the normal modifier once.

Natural-1 Complications

A natural 1 can create a fictionally appropriate complication that moves the scene forward. It is not an automatic slapstick failure and it is not permission for arbitrary punishment. The rule applies to PCs and NPCs.

Potions

  • Drink a potion yourself: Bonus Action.
  • Administer a potion to another creature: Action.
  • Healing potions restore their maximum listed healing.
  • Consuming more than one potion within one in-game hour triggers the established Potion Toxicity check/table.

Quick Checks in Combat

A brief observational or interpretive check may be free when it represents a quick glance or immediate read of the scene. Sustained searching, negotiation, detailed manipulation or significant multitasking can cost an Action or carry a situational penalty. The cost follows what the character is actually attempting.

Stacking Inspiration

Inspiration awards can stack. They are especially appropriate when a player commits to a trait, ideal, bond or flaw in a way that meaningfully complicates the character's life; accepts a detrimental consequence because it is right for the character; or creates strong collaborative roleplay.

Blind Death Saves

Death saves are secret/blind. The rest of the table does not know the exact success/failure count while the character is unconscious.

pages.name: Table Policy & Safety
pages.html:
Player Facing

Table Policy

The social contract for a collaborative campaign.

  • Respect people in and out of character. Personal attacks, derogatory language and belittling are not acceptable.
  • Listen when someone has the floor. Give character moments, descriptions and decisions room to land.
  • Stay engaged. Real-life interruptions happen; prolonged unrelated browsing, phone use or side conversations should not become routine.
  • Arrive ready. Have access to Foundry and know your core features well enough to take a turn without rebuilding your character at the table.
  • Keep rulings moving. Questions and respectful corrections are welcome. Once a ruling is made for the scene, move on and revisit it after the session if necessary.
  • Share spotlight. Busy social scenes can become effectively turn-based. Give everyone room to act and speak.
  • Characters can argue; players remain collaborators.
  • PvP is exceptional and consent-based. Theft from another PC, harmful magic, deliberate friendly fire or major betrayal should not be sprung on another player as a surprise.
  • Step away when needed. If it is urgent, simply go. No scene is more important than a real person.
Player Facing

Open Door, Boundaries & Feedback

Simple tools for keeping the campaign comfortable without interrupting its momentum.

Baseline Boundaries

  • Line: sexual violence.
  • Line: direct harm to children as entertainment or graphic content.
  • Line: graphic torture descriptions.
  • Veil: sexual activity fades to black.

Open Door

Anyone can say pause, say hold on, message the DM privately, or step away. No justification is required in the moment. The scene can be reframed, skipped, retconned or moved past. New boundaries can be added privately at any time.

Campaign Content

Franchise Wars can include corporate exploitation, predatory contracts, workplace mistreatment, fantasy violence, undead and monsters, magical coercion, some body-horror-adjacent magical incidents, infernal/legalistic supernatural threats, and satire of consumption, employment and wealth.

Stars & Wishes

Most sessions close with a quick calibration:

  • Star: something another player, the DM, a scene or the game did that worked well.
  • Wish: something you want more of, less of, or hope to see in future.

Wishes are forward-looking guidance for making the campaign better.

pages.html:
Player Handbook

Pregenerated Contractors

Five level-1 contractors ready to sign.

Each is in the Actors sidebar under Pregenerated Contractors. Ask the GM to give you ownership. Class, species, background, gear, class features and spells are filled in from your dnd5e compendiums when the module imports; check the class item for skill and equipment choices.

@FWLink[Actor|fw.actor.pregen.brick]{Brick Dunmore}

Human Fighter 1 · Soldier · Neutral Good

Former night-door bouncer at a Murder King drive-thru. Quit the day the mascot asked him to “escort out” a crying child.

Wants: A steady wage and a job where hitting things is the honest part.
Won’t sell: He will not throw out anyone who has nowhere else to go.
Trinket: A Murder King name badge with “BRICK — HAPPY TO HELP” scratched to “HAPPY TO QUIT”.

STR 15 · DEX 13 · CON 14 · INT 8 · WIS 12 · CHA 10 (standard array + background bonuses)

@FWLink[Actor|fw.actor.pregen.odalie]{Odalie Quillfeather}

Elf Wizard 1 · Sage · Lawful Neutral

An actuary dismissed from Head Office for “excessive accuracy”. She noticed a number in a contract that should not have been there.

Wants: To find out what the number meant.
Won’t sell: She will not sign anything she has not read twice.
Trinket: A brass slide rule with one bead missing, which she insists matters.

STR 8 · DEX 14 · CON 13 · INT 15 · WIS 12 · CHA 10 (standard array + background bonuses)

@FWLink[Actor|fw.actor.pregen.margery]{Sister Margery Tallow}

Dwarf Cleric 1 · Acolyte · Neutral Good

Ran a free healing table outside the Goodberry’s pharmacy until she received a letter about “unlicensed use of a protected wellness term”.

Wants: Enough money to keep the free table running.
Won’t sell: She will never charge a patient.
Trinket: A chipped tin mug that once held the tips jar. It is still the tips jar.

STR 14 · DEX 8 · CON 15 · INT 10 · WIS 15 · CHA 12 (standard array + background bonuses)

@FWLink[Actor|fw.actor.pregen.nim]{Nim Pocket}

Halfling Rogue 1 · Criminal · Chaotic Good

A loss-prevention officer at Wand-Mart who prevented a loss by giving the stolen bread back to the family who took it.

Wants: Proof that the shelves have more than one set of owners.
Won’t sell: Nim never takes from someone who has less.
Trinket: A store-security whistle that has never been blown.

STR 8 · DEX 15 · CON 14 · INT 12 · WIS 13 · CHA 10 (standard array + background bonuses)

@FWLink[Actor|fw.actor.pregen.jingle]{Jingle Vane}

Tiefling Bard 1 · Entertainer · Chaotic Neutral

Wrote the Golden Orcs jingle that every child in Brandmere hums. Signed away the rights for a free meal. The meal was cold.

Wants: To write one song nobody can own.
Won’t sell: Jingle will not sing for a company again. (Probably.)
Trinket: The original jingle on a napkin, with the signature line torn off.

STR 8 · DEX 14 · CON 13 · INT 10 · WIS 12 · CHA 15 (standard array + background bonuses)

pages.name: Orientation
pages.html:
Player Facing

Welcome to Franchise Wars

QuestRabbit contractor orientation: what this campaign is and what your character needs.

Brandmere is a city where adventuring has been franchised. Every major chain has a flagship, every holding company has a tower, and QuestRabbit Adventuring Solutions has found a way to take thirty percent of danger.

Your Starting Position

You are a level 1 adventurer joining a small contractor team. QuestRabbit does not own your character, your beliefs or your loyalty. It provides contracts, ratings, specialist credentials and access to work. What you do with those opportunities is yours.

Expect missing employees, magical workplace incidents, cursed products, hostile takeovers, monsters in storerooms, franchise disputes, corporate espionage, strange customers and jobs that technically never existed.

The Campaign

  • Levels 1–20.
  • Corporate fantasy-comedy with real consequences.
  • Combat, investigation, social manoeuvring, exploration, contracts, moral choices and recurring NPCs.
  • Characters may be ambitious, cynical, idealistic, greedy, anti-corporate, desperate, loyal or opportunistic.
  • The satire targets power and systems. Ordinary employees are people caught in those systems.

What Your Character Needs

  • A believable reason to take paid adventuring work.
  • A reason to cooperate with the other PCs.
  • At least one desire strong enough to create difficult choices.
  • At least one principle, relationship or part of themselves they do not want to sell.
  • Enough flexibility to remain part of an ensemble campaign.

Character Creation

  • Starting level: 1.
  • Ability scores: Standard Array or 27-point buy.
  • Normal class/background equipment.
  • Choose one small personal trinket connected to a former employer, family, craft, vice, ambition, failure or important relationship.
  • Your QuestRabbit company position is chosen separately from your class and background.
Orientation Question

Before QuestRabbit, I took dangerous work because…

pages.name: Using Acquisitions Incorporated
pages.html:
Player Facing

QuestRabbit Specialist Positions

The official Acquisitions Incorporated franchise subsystem, re-skinned for Brandmere.

Rules Source. Use the official Acquisitions Incorporated sourcebook for the exact company-position mechanics, rank features, specialist equipment and franchise-task rules. Franchise Wars references those mechanics rather than reproducing proprietary rules text.

Each PC chooses one company position where practical. The position is an additional organisational role; it does not replace class or background.

PositionQuestRabbit FunctionCharacter Question
CartographerRoutes, mapping, travel and getting the team where the contract says it is.When did following your directions once get somebody hurt?
DecisionistVotes, group decisions, morale and resolving indecision when nobody wants responsibility.What decision do you still regret?
DocumancerContracts, records, paperwork, clauses and making bureaucracy useful before it becomes lethal.Why are you suspicious of contracts?
HoardspersonResources, loot, inventory and the uncomfortable question of who gets what.What possession could you never bring yourself to sell?
LoremongerResearch, names, history, institutional memory and facts somebody hoped had been forgotten.What secret do you already know that you should not?
ObviatorThreat analysis, tactical weaknesses and making obstacles stop being obstacles.When did destroying something make the situation worse?
OccultantDanger, death, supernatural consequence and the strange accounting of what a life costs.Why are you unusually comfortable around death?
SecretarianContacts, communications, reputation, information and making the right person hear the right version of events.When did a lie save somebody?

Franchise Wars Adaptation

  • QuestRabbit issues the specialist authority/equipment while the party operates through the Warren.
  • Position rank follows the official franchise-rank progression in the sourcebook.
  • Specialist items remain role-specific property rather than ordinary shared loot.
  • Official Franchise Tasks and Downtime can be used between contracts for research, marketing, schmoozing, headquarters work and related operations.
  • The party's early operational base is its QuestRabbit workspace at the Warren. A dedicated headquarters can develop through play.
  • The QuestRabbit thirty-percent commission represents early agency overhead. Do not also apply a second layer of low-level franchise operating costs while the party remains a QuestRabbit contractor team.
  • Rabbit Rating, Leverage, Commons Tally, Receipts, Folios and Board control are separate Franchise Wars campaign systems.

pages.name: Three Jobs Before QuestRabbit
pages.html:
Player Facing

Communal Backstory Workshop

Build the contractor team by creating the jobs they survived before the campaign began.

Opening Round

Complete the sentence: Before QuestRabbit, I took dangerous work because…

These jobs happened before S01. They are not secret campaign missions; they are the shared résumé that explains why this team already knows how to work together.

Job One — The Job We Brag About

Create one low-level contract that genuinely went well.

  1. Who hired you?
  2. What was the apparently simple job?
  3. What unexpected thing made it dangerous?
  4. Who took charge?
  5. Who did something impressive nobody else could have done?
  6. Whose mistake nearly ruined it?
  7. What ordinary person remembers you fondly because of what happened?
  8. What trophy, receipt, broken object, scar or ridiculous souvenir survived?
  9. What exaggerated version of the story do you tell strangers?

Job Two — The Job We Never Mention

Create the group's shared professional embarrassment.

  1. What did the client actually ask for?
  2. What did the party misunderstand?
  3. What was destroyed, lost, awakened, released, delivered to the wrong person or accidentally signed?
  4. Who tried to warn everyone?
  5. Who took the blame publicly?
  6. Who actually caused it?
  7. Who still has an unpaid bill, grievance or legal complaint because of it?
  8. Which rival contractor knows what really happened?
  9. What phrase causes the whole party to go quiet because of this job?

Job Three — The Job We Did for Free

Create the moment that proves what the team is like when nobody is paying.

  1. Who needed help?
  2. Why was there no money in it?
  3. Who first said yes?
  4. Who objected and then helped anyway?
  5. What promise did the party make?
  6. What did helping cost them?
  7. Which NPC, family, worker, neighbourhood, guild or small business still remembers?
  8. What small gift or keepsake did they receive instead of payment?
  9. Would they make the same choice again?

Team Formation

  • How did the characters first meet?
  • Why did they choose to take a second job together?
  • What makes each character useful to the team that has nothing to do with damage output?
  • Which two characters disagree most often, and why does that not break the group?
  • Who normally speaks to a client?
  • Who reads the fine print?
  • Who is trusted with the money?
  • Who gets blamed when there is no obvious culprit?
  • What is the party's unwritten rule?
  • Why are they applying to QuestRabbit now?

One Shared Keepsake

Choose one small object from the old days that the team keeps together. It should be small enough to sit in the eventual office and meaningful enough that losing it would hurt.

pages.name: Character-to-Character Bonds
pages.html:
Player Facing

Character-to-Character Bonds

Give every PC relationships that existed before the first campaign contract.

Go around the table. Each player answers at least two prompts involving different PCs.

  • Which character have you known longest?
  • Which character owes you money?
  • Which character knows something embarrassing about you?
  • Which character did you initially dislike but now trust?
  • Which character have you lied to?
  • Which character has seen you at your absolute worst?
  • Which character would you trust with your life but not your wallet?
  • Which character's approval secretly matters to you?
  • Which character did you once cover for?
  • Which character are you slightly jealous of?

Relationships do not need to be symmetrical. One character may believe another is their closest friend while the feeling is not fully returned.

Create One Shared NPC

Invent one ordinary person in Brandmere who already knows the team: a tavern owner, retired adventurer, street-food vendor, shopkeeper, former employer, neighbour, union representative, teacher, courier, craftsperson or similar.

Round the Table

Why does this person know your character?

pages.name: Personnel File
pages.html:
Player Facing

Contractor Personnel File

Questions designed to give the DM material that can return as real campaign consequences.

Core Personnel Questions

  1. What do you want badly enough to risk your life for money?
  2. What do you believe having enough money would actually fix?
  3. What is your relationship with authority? Obedient, cynical, rebellious, manipulative, aspirational, frightened, something else?
  4. What is the worst professional or personal failure you have had?
  5. What principle do you claim you would never compromise?
  6. What secret could seriously damage your reputation if your colleagues learned it?
  7. Who outside the party matters enough that you would abandon a contract to help them?
  8. What kind of person immediately earns your sympathy?
  9. What kind of person immediately earns your contempt?
  10. What does success look like to you right now?

Private Questions for the DM

These can be answered privately after the communal workshop.

  1. What is something your character desperately wants but should not receive easily?
  2. What unresolved relationship from their past would you enjoy seeing appear?
  3. What mistake from their past could realistically come back to hurt them?
  4. What belief would be interesting for the campaign to challenge?
  5. Is there something you would enjoy the DM revealing about your character that the other PCs initially do not know?

Quick Eight

If time is short, the DM needs at least these eight pieces:

  • What can a bad employer exploit because you want it so badly?
  • What will you not sell, betray or compromise even for life-changing money?
  • Who depends on you?
  • Who do you owe — money, loyalty, an apology or a favour?
  • What failure still influences your decisions?
  • What flaw gets worse under stress?
  • What secret would hurt your reputation if made public?
  • What would make you walk away from QuestRabbit?

pages.name: Hook Mapping
pages.html:
GM Only

DM Hook Integration

Turn Session 0 answers into recurring Franchise Wars material without exposing the campaign machinery.

Player MaterialCampaign Connections
Authority / institution traumaQuestRabbit bureaucracy, Crown & Cleaver executives, inspections, contracts, arbitration and institutional power.
Money / security / statusRaises, retainers, executive access, Hoard Syndicate wealth, Rabbit Rating perks and offers that should be genuinely tempting.
Worker sympathy / anti-exploitationUnderpaid staff, labour disputes, the Old Independents, small businesses and Marda Hobb.
Family business / craft / local rootsThe Old Independents' Quarter, the Rows, Harbour & Driftwood or another Brandmere district threatened or tempted by expansion.
Contracts / law / bureaucracyDocumancy, Arbitration Court, Guild of Scriveners, disputed clauses, Folios and recurring paperwork.
Fame / storytelling / public recognitionMcGuffin Narrative Holdings, Songbird Quarter, public reviews, Rabbit Rating publicity and corporate PR.
Planar / magical backgroundPlanar Quay, Planar Hospitality Group, strange imports and extraplanar clients.
Death / undeath / griefRestaurant Necromancy Group, Nine Circles Hospitality, undead workers and questions about personhood as an asset.
Food / hospitality / retail backgroundConnect a family, former employer or rival directly to a franchise or an independent business.
Shame / professional failureA rival contractor knows enough to needle the PC but not enough to invalidate the character.
A person they protectPlace that NPC somewhere the campaign revisits naturally. Do not default to kidnapping; let consequences reach them in varied ways.

Session 0 Deliverables to Record

  • Final character names and player names.
  • Class, background and species.
  • Company position.
  • Core motivation and core flaw.
  • Hard line the character will not cross.
  • Temptation Corporate could exploit.
  • Important NPCs and places.
  • The three shared jobs and their consequences.
  • Party relationships and communal keepsake.
  • Rival/debt.
  • Safety notes.
  • Stars & Wishes.

Use the Material Early

Do not wait until Act IV to acknowledge the backstories. Put at least one Session 0 NPC, debt, promise, rival, former employer or personal ambition into the first several contracts. The players should learn immediately that what they created matters.

pages.name: Systems
pages.html:
Campaign Systems

The campaign uses five tracking systems. None is complicated; together they make every side contract matter to the finale. Keep a single sheet—the Contractor File—on which you record all five.

Contract Grades

GradeLevelsTypical WorkBase Pay
Copper 1–4 Pest control, deliveries, missing employees, petty espionage 25–150 gp
Silver 5–8 Monster nests, sabotage, dangerous acquisitions, supernatural workplace incidents 300–1,500 gp
Gold 9–12 Interplanar procurement, corporate warfare, powerful magical entities 2,000–8,000 gp
Platinum 13–16 Demonic mergers, dimensional monopolies, ancient franchises, catastrophes 10,000–40,000 gp
Black Card 17–20 Jobs that technically never existed Payment in kind

The 30%. QuestRabbit deducts thirty per cent of every fee. Pip Ashworth will explain that this is industry standard. It is not. Players who negotiate directly with a client (Persuasion DC 15 [[/check skill=per dc=15]] + the grade's tier) can cut QuestRabbit out—but a contract taken off the board doesn't count toward the Rabbit Rating.

The Rabbit Rating

The party shares a single rating from one to five stars. It begins at one star when they sign the Contractor Agreement in S1. Publicly, it's a customer-satisfaction score that unlocks better contracts. Secretly, it measures how much ordinary people trust the party—and it is the metaphysical threshold that makes their signatures valid for the Material Plane.

StarsUnlocksHidden Meaning (DM)
★ Copper contracts; a badge Known to one neighbourhood
★★ Silver contracts; QuestRabbit expense account (50 gp/month) Trusted by a district
★★★ Gold contracts; a Folio page is opened in the party's name (S10) Trusted by a city
★★★★ Platinum contracts; a private office at the Warren Trusted by a nation
★★★★★ Black Card; an invitation to the AGM (S20) Representatives of the Commons: signature valid for the Material Plane

Earning Stars. The rating is not XP. It rises at the milestones shown in the spine (S2, S5, S10, S15 and S20 each add a star if the party completed the act's missions) and it can rise early if the party does something that makes the public love them. It never falls below the star count the spine requires—the Ledger won't allow it. Players who try to tank their rating deliberately (rudeness, sabotage, refusing jobs) discover that one-star reviews simply don't post. This is the first clue, around Act III, that the rating isn't what it seems.

The Mandate (optional). If the party cuts ties with QuestRabbit, the rating continues under a new name: the Mandate, tracked in the Folio page Wand-Mart opens for them in S10. Nothing changes except the font.

Leverage

Leverage represents dirt, debts, favours and secrets the party holds over a specific corporation. Track Leverage separately for each of the ten Board umbrellas plus Creation & Company. Every contract in this book lists a Leverage target; completing it with the truth exposed (not buried) grants 1 Leverage against that target. Spine missions grant the amounts they list.

Spending Leverage. A point can be spent at any time to gain one of the following against the target corporation, its staff or its directors:

  • Advantage. Advantage on one Charisma check, or on one argument in the Clause Debate (S24).
  • Access. A door opens: a meeting, a warehouse, a file, a board member's private dining room.
  • Cover. The corporation's security looks the other way for one scene.
  • Proxy. In S23, 2 Leverage against an umbrella lets the party demand its director's proxy. The director may refuse, but must then be dealt with in person.

Losing Leverage. Leverage is lost when the party is bought off (accepting a “bonus” from the target), when their evidence is destroyed, or when they use it and the target retaliates—at your discretion, one point spent in a heavy-handed way costs one more.

The Commons Tally

The Grand Ledger records only written agreements. Handshakes, favours done for free, gifts, promises made in a tavern and kept—these are invisible to it. Creation & Company can't see them, can't buy them and can't cancel them.

Whenever the party helps someone and refuses payment, or makes an unwritten promise and keeps it, record that person or group on the Commons Tally. Named NPCs count as one; a union, a neighbourhood or a guild counts as one. Most side contracts note where a Tally ally can be won instead of gold.

  • In play. Tally allies show up. Call on one per session for a small favour—no roll.
  • In S23. Tally allies attend the Extraordinary General Meeting as observers. For every five, one wavering director has disadvantage to refuse the party.
  • In S24. Each Tally ally present can act as a witness. Clauses with no Receipt can be voided by three witnesses in place of a DC 25 argument. The Held in Common ending requires at least twenty.

Receipts

A Receipt is proof. Twelve spine missions each produce one specific Receipt that voids one clause of the Final Contract; a thirteenth (Incident Report 77-B) is found in the first hour of the campaign and voids the clause that makes the party signatories. Other missions produce Receipts that weaken Tallis Vend or open the way forward.

Receipts are physical. Put them on index cards and hand them to the players. Lose track of one and it's gone; destroyed Receipts can be reconstructed only by a DC 25 argument or three Tally witnesses. By level 20 the players should have a stack of cards they've been carrying for a year, and should suddenly understand why.

Folios

A Folio is a branch ledger: a lesser book that synchronises with the Grand Ledger. Every major corporation keeps them. Entries written in a Folio become true within that corporation's holdings. The party's first Folio is found in S10 (Wand-Mart); see Appendix B for the magic item. Folios are how the party learns the rules of the Ledger before they ever see it—and how you can dramatise “paperwork is reality” at every level.

The Board

Creation & Company rules through a Board of ten directors, one per umbrella corporation, plus the Chairman. Tallis Vend controls 51% through their proxies. In S23, the party needs six seats flipped (the director votes against Vend) or removed (the director is gone and their proxy void). Each umbrella's dossier in Chapter 5 lists exactly how its seat turns. Track the Board on the Contractor File from S8 onward; the players should be able to see the vote coming for two whole acts.

Chapter 3

pages.name: Gazetteer
pages.html:
Brandmere, City of Franchises

Brandmere is a harbour city of two hundred thousand souls built on a river delta, where three trade roads meet the sea. It was an ordinary market town until, about a century ago, it became the first city in the realm to grant franchise charters. Now it is the commercial capital of the world: every chain has a flagship here, every holding company a tower, and every street a loyalty scheme. The city's motto, carved over the Old Gate, reads Fides et Mercatura—“Trust and Trade.” Someone has since added a ™.

Brandmere at a Glance

Government The Chamber of Commerce, a council of franchise owners weighted by market share. The Lord Mayor, Esmond Tallow-Pryce, is a figurehead who does not realise his office has been leased.
Law The City Watch, most of whom are paid in Dungeon Donuts vouchers. Serious crimes are resolved by the Arbitration Court on Guild Row, where both sides pay a filing fee and the higher fee wins most ties.
Currency Standard coin, plus loyalty points, which are accepted in more shops than gold. Loyalty points cannot be converted back.
News The Brandmere Crier (independent, tiny, brave) and The Market Herald (owned by McGuffin Narrative Holdings, very large, always has a twist).
Religion The old temples still stand but rent their forecourts to kiosks. In Act III the Temple of the Healing Hand is sued for trademark infringement (S12).

Districts

Guild Row

Offices, courts and the Warren, QuestRabbit's cheerful burrow-tower, whose job boards glow when a contract posts. Harriet Hopwell's office is on the top floor; Pip Ashworth's desk is in the lobby beside a ficus. The Arbitration Court and the Guild of Scriveners are across the square.

Hook. A contractor who hasn't been seen in a month still has a job listed as “in progress.” Pip is worried.

Drive-Thru Row

A mile of fast-food flagships under hanging signs, open all night: THAC0 Spell, Murder King, Wight Castle, Five Wights, the Brandmere Grand Tusks. Carts queue in the road. The THAC0 Spell flagship, managed by Hollis Quench, is where the campaign begins, and where the Franchise Below lies waiting.

Hook. A drive-thru speaking-tube has started taking orders from someone who isn't there.

Corporate Row

The towers. Crown & Cleaver's black-glass spire, the Arcane Beverage International Reserve Roastery, the Hoard Syndicate's vault-bank. Upmarket franchises serve people who never eat anywhere else. Every building has a lobby with a fountain and a receptionist with a clipboard.

Hook. Every clock on Corporate Row stopped at the same minute. The towers want it kept quiet.

The Old Independents' Quarter

Crooked streets, family taverns and shops that have refused every franchise agreement. The heart is Tallow Lane and the Tankard & Tallow, Marda Hobb's tavern and the unofficial headquarters of the Last Independents. By Act V it's the party's war room. The Quarter shrinks every year; people who sign franchise deals here tend to vanish.

Hook. Marda asks the party to walk a new baker home each night. No payment. (Commons Tally.)

The Harbour & Driftwood Quarter

Docks, fish markets and the Codfather's Harbour Fry. Beyond the breakwater, a district sank when the coast flooded forty years ago; its rooftops show at low tide, and a Golden Tusks sign still glows beneath the water (S21). The Driftwood Quarter's taverns cater to sailors and sahuagin traders.

Hook. A letter arrives, dated tomorrow, postmarked from below the harbour.

The Songbird Quarter

Music halls, bard bars and all-night cafés: Hard Bard Café, Bard to the Bone, Wok & Roll Initiative. Street performers need a licence from McGuffin Narrative Holdings, which owns the phrase “once upon a time.”

Hook. Every busker in the Quarter is playing the same song, and none of them wrote it.

The Rows

A grid of specialty streets named for trades—Adventurers' Row, Brewer's Row, Tinkers' Row, Stonewall Row, Gamblers' Row—each dominated by a franchise that pushed out the craft it's named for. Probability Brands Group owns most of Gamblers' Row. The dice are loaded. So is the rent.

Hook. The last independent blacksmith on Adventurers' Row has been offered a sum of money that is exactly his lifetime earnings to the copper.

The Retail Park

Outside the old walls, on land that used to be farms: the Wand-Mart Supercentre, Quest Buy, the CostCo-op warehouse and the IKEA Mimic showroom, whose car park is larger than some villages. Caravans come from three countries to buy in bulk. Nobody who works nights here talks about the Showroom.

Hook. The Retail Park has a new aisle. It wasn't there yesterday, and it's longer on the inside.

Camp Brandmere & the Tollgate Pass

The fortified depot of the Little Caesars Legion, which treats pizza delivery as a military occupation. Beyond it, the Tollgate Pass climbs into the mountains, where the Summit Tusks franchise sits on a peak that sees every road in the realm.

Hook. The Legion has begun “delivering” to villages that didn't order anything.

Planar Quay

A dock that isn't on the river. Portals to the City of Brass, Mechanus and the Astral are leased by the Planar Hospitality Group, with customs officers who check both your luggage and your soul. Trader Djinn's and Plane Inn keep flagships here.

Hook. Customs has impounded a crate addressed to the party. It is ticking, in a language.

Recurring Faces

NPCRoleArc
Pip Ashworth Harengon QuestRabbit liaison; the party's handler Genuinely kind; learns the truth in Act IV; walks into the Signing Room holding his own Clause 77-B (S24).
Harriet Hopwell Founder and CEO of QuestRabbit Believes in her company. Sold it ninety-five years ago without knowing to whom. Can revoke the party's rating at the AGM (S20).
Hollis Quench THAC0 Spell night manager Kept the original Incident Report 77-B. The campaign's first informant.
Veronique Salt Vice President, Crown & Cleaver Holdings Brilliant, ruthless, ambitious. Signs off on the S1 recall. Becomes the party's rival, then their coup partner (S15, S23). Might betray them.
Marda Hobb Owner of the Tankard & Tallow; leader of the Last Independents Refuses Murder King in S8. Her tavern becomes the party's war room.
Mortimer Pell The murdered Murder King mascot performer Walks after closing (S2). Knows who killed him and why. Remembers the original King.
Counsel Ixabeth Vorr Erinyes attorney, Nine Circles Hospitality Hell resents being acquired. She switches sides after S13 and files the motion for audit (S20).
Team Deliverables Rival contractor party from GigGoblin Take credit, steal jobs, level alongside the party. Their arc ends with them either signing for Creation & Company or not (see Bestiary).
Tallis Vend Chairman, Creation & Company Unseen until S20. Polite, grey and certain. Owns himself.

Chapter 4

pages.html:
GM ONLY

Mission at a Glance

Scenes@FWLink[JournalEntry|fw.mission.S01|Scene 1 — Onboarding at the Warren]{Scene 1 — Onboarding at the Warren} — @FWLink[Scene|fw.scene.fw-a1-01-questrabbit-warren]{map}
@FWLink[JournalEntry|fw.mission.S01|Scene 2 — Lunch Rush]{Scene 2 — Lunch Rush} — @FWLink[Scene|fw.scene.fw-a1-02-thac0-spell-flagship]{map}
@FWLink[JournalEntry|fw.mission.S01|Scene 3 — The Ingredient]{Scene 3 — The Ingredient} — @FWLink[Scene|fw.scene.fw-a1-02-thac0-spell-flagship]{map}
@FWLink[JournalEntry|fw.mission.S01|Scene 4 — The Cellar with Two Doors]{Scene 4 — The Cellar with Two Doors} — @FWLink[Scene|fw.scene.fw-a1-03-thac0-cellar]{map}
@FWLink[JournalEntry|fw.mission.S01|Scene 5 — Corporate Resolution]{Scene 5 — Corporate Resolution} — @FWLink[Scene|fw.scene.fw-a1-02-thac0-spell-flagship]{map}
Key NPCs@FWLink[Actor|fw.actor.recurring.pip-ashworth]{Pip Ashworth}, @FWLink[Actor|fw.actor.staff.FR-01]{Hollis Quench}, @FWLink[Actor|fw.actor.recurring.dobbs]{Dobbs}, @FWLink[Actor|fw.actor.bestiary.veronique-salt]{Veronique Salt (by signature only)}
Receipt@FWLink[Item|fw.item.receipt.S01]{Incident Report 77-B (original)}

Synopsis

The characters sign their QuestRabbit Contractor Agreements at the Warren—including a shimmering clause, 77-B, that appoints them "Representatives of the Commons for purposes of future transactions." Pip Ashworth, their cheerful harengon handler, sends them to their first Copper job: THAC0 Spell's Drive-Thru Row flagship, where the limited-time Wild Burrito is turning one customer in six into a minor magical disaster.

During a chaotic lunch rush the party keeps order, tastes the menu and traces the surges to a humming jar of red powder labelled Promotional Seasoning — C&C Supply. Night manager Hollis Quench quietly takes them down to the cellar, where an iron door older than the building's foundations stands warm and locked; behind it, faintly, a till rings. Hollis gives them the original Incident Report 77-B—the account of a line cook, Dobbs, who walked through that door and never came back.

Head Office sends a courier with a recall memo and asks for the report. Whether the party hands over the original or a forgery is the first real decision of the campaign—and the original is the first of the Receipts that will one day void @FWLink[JournalEntry|fw.finalcontract]{the Final Contract}.

Background — DM Only

THAC0 Spell is owned by @FWLink[JournalEntry|fw.corp.CO-07]{Probability Brands Group}, which in turn answers to Creation & Company. The "C&C Supply" stamp is not Crown & Cleaver, as everyone will assume; it is Creation & Company's procurement arm, which shipped a single jar of very old wild-magic spice to the flagship to see what would happen to customer behaviour. (PBG's data collection is real: a tally sheet in the manager's office records surge outcomes per table.)

The flagship was built on top of something far older. The iron door in its cellar is the back door of the First Shop, the Franchise Below (S14), and the till that rings behind it is the original register of all commerce. The spice reacted to it; that is why the surges are worse near the kitchen stairs. Dobbs, the line cook in Incident Report 77-B, opened that door eleven years ago and is still behind the counter on the other side.

Clause 77-B of the QuestRabbit Contractor Agreement and Incident Report 77-B share a number by accident of filing—or not. Nobody should notice yet. The Report is the Receipt that voids Clause 77-B (Signature Authority) in S24. If the party hands over the original, Hollis secretly kept a carbon copy, so the Receipt can still be recovered later—but at a cost (a favour, a risk, or a lowered Rabbit Rating).

Running This Mission

  • This is a tone-setter. Lean into the comedy of corporate fast food—then let the cellar door land with real unease. The golden rule: the jokes are on the corporations, never on the workers.
  • Introduce Pip Ashworth as warmly as you can. Players should love him; it matters in Acts IV and V.
  • The lunch rush is a "keep order" challenge rather than a fight. Run it as three rounds of escalating chaos; let every character have a moment.
  • Team Deliverables arrive halfway through. Use them to teach the Credit Theft rule: if the party can't prove who did the work, the Rabbit Rating star goes to the rivals.
  • End the session on the choice of which report to hand over. Don't rush it; let the players talk.

Threads In and Out

  • In: @FWLink[JournalEntry|fw.session0.gm]{Session 0} hooks, the characters' Personnel Files, and the Contractor Agreement.
  • Out: Hollis becomes an informant; the iron door opens in @FWLink[JournalEntry|fw.mission.S14]{S14 — The Franchise Below}; Veronique Salt signed the recall and appears in @FWLink[JournalEntry|fw.mission.S02]{S02}; the Report voids Clause 77-B in @FWLink[JournalEntry|fw.mission.S24]{S24}.

The Hook

Read Aloud — The Hook@FWChat[narrate]{Send to chat}

The Warren smells of cedar shavings, fresh ink and very strong tea. Beneath a vaulted burrow ceiling, a job board the size of a barn door bristles with pinned slips, each one stamped with a rabbit in a tiny helmet. Somewhere a bell dings, and a harengon in a waistcoat bounds toward you with a clipboard held over his head like a trophy.

"New contractors! Oh, this is the best part of my day. I'm Pip—Pip Ashworth, your liaison, handler, cheerleader and, legally, your point of contact for all grievances. You'll need to sign these. In quadruplicate. Don't worry about the small print; Legal wrote it, and they're very thorough!"

Pip produces four copies of the Contractor Agreement per character, a QuestRabbit Contractor Badge each, and a job slip still warm from the board. Hand out the Contractor Agreement handout (see Scene 1).

pages.name: Scene 1 — Onboarding at the Warren
pages.html:
GM ONLY

Map: @FWLink[Scene|fw.scene.fw-a1-01-questrabbit-warren]{Open battlemap}
When: Morning, the first day of employment
Present: @FWLink[Actor|fw.actor.recurring.pip-ashworth]{Pip Ashworth}
Handouts: @FWLink[JournalEntry|fw.handouts.S01|QuestRabbit Contractor Agreement (excerpt)]{QuestRabbit Contractor Agreement (excerpt)} @FWShow[fw.handouts.S01|QuestRabbit Contractor Agreement (excerpt)]{Show to players} · @FWLink[JournalEntry|fw.handouts.S01|Job Slip — THAC0 Spell (Copper)]{Job Slip — THAC0 Spell (Copper)} @FWShow[fw.handouts.S01|Job Slip — THAC0 Spell (Copper)]{Show to players}

Read Aloud@FWChat[narrate]{Send to chat}

Pip ushers you to a round table in the central burrow, beneath the board of tiny helmeted rabbits. Around you, other contractors—a dwarf with three swords, an elf asleep in her soup, a goblin trio in matching tabards—sign forms with the glazed patience of the recently hired.

Pip clears his throat, holds the Contractor Agreement at arm's length, and begins to read in the bright, sing-song voice of someone who has done this four hundred times. "Clause one: the Contractor agrees to adventure. Clause two: the Contractor agrees that QuestRabbit receives thirty percent of all fees, gratuities, treasure, and—oh, that's new—'consideration in kind'. Clauses three through seventy-seven I am not permitted to read aloud, which is fine, because they're very boring. Clause seventy-seven-B…" He pauses, squints, and turns the page over. "Skip. Sign here, here, here, initial here, and here."

DM Description

The Warren is QuestRabbit's headquarters: a hillside office built like a burrow, with a parquet-floored central lobby, round side-burrows for Legal, onboarding and training, and a small archive. It is cosy, busy and genuinely friendly. Nobody here is evil; they simply believe in the product.

Each character receives a Contractor Agreement (the handout), a @FWLink[Item|fw.item.magic.07]{QuestRabbit Contractor Badge}, and a one-star Rabbit Rating, which Pip chalks up on the star board above the job board with enormous ceremony. Pip then pulls the THAC0 Spell slip off the board and hands it over.

Clause 77-B is the hidden heart of the scene. A character who reads the full Agreement or casts detect magic notices that one line shimmers faintly gold, as though written in a different ink: "Signatory is appointed Representative of the Commons for purposes of future transactions." Pip shrugs: "Legal wrote that. They're very thorough!" He genuinely does not know what it means.

Features of the Area

Job Board
Hundreds of pinned slips sorted by grade—Copper, Silver, Gold, Platinum and one sealed Black Card envelope pinned at the very top that nobody will touch. A successful look at it reveals jobs for every franchise in the city; seed future side contracts here.
Star Board
A slate above the job board listing every contracted party and its Rabbit Rating in chalk stars. The party's name goes up at one star. At the top, chalked in faded old-fashioned script, is a single entry that has never been erased: "The Last Five-Star Party — ★★★★★" (S16).
Legal Burrow (west)
Filing cabinets to the ceiling and two clerks who never look up. If asked about 77-B: "We don't draft them, we file them. They come down from Head Office pre-signed by the Board."
Onboarding Burrow (east)
Pip's domain: a long table, a samovar, and a framed photograph of Pip with QuestRabbit founder Harriet Hopwell, both beaming.
Carrot Lounge & Training Hall
A sofa lounge with a self-serve carrot-cake counter, and a training burrow with armour stands and a chalk circle for practice sparring. Good places for characters to bond.

Playing the NPCs

@FWLink[Actor|fw.actor.recurring.pip-ashworth]{Pip Ashworth}. Bounces on the balls of his feet, speaks in exclamation marks, and remembers every contractor's birthday. He hates conflict and will try to resolve any argument with cake. If pressed about the 30% cut, he says, earnestly, "It covers your insurance! And the badge! And me!"

Checks & Roll Requests

SituationRollResult
Reading the full Agreement (every page)[[/check skill=inv dc=20]] @FWCheck[S01|skill=inv dc=20|Reading the whole Contractor Agreement]{Request}Spots Clause 77-B shimmering and notices the phrase "Representative of the Commons". On 25+, also notices it is signed in advance by "the Board".
Casting detect magic on the paperwork—Automatic: Clause 77-B glows faint gold; divination-school aura, very old.
Reading Pip[[/check skill=ins dc=10]] @FWCheck[S01|skill=ins dc=10|Is Pip hiding anything?]{Request}He is completely sincere. He has never read Clause 77-B either.
Asking the Legal clerks[[/check skill=per dc=13]] @FWCheck[S01|skill=per dc=13|Charming the Legal burrow]{Request}They mention the clauses arrive "pre-signed by the Board" and that "the Board" is not QuestRabbit's board.

Lines to Steal

Pip: “Every great adventuring career starts with a Copper! I started with a Copper. Well. I started in the mail room. But it was copper-coloured.”
Pip: “One star! Look at you. Everybody starts at one star. Five stars is—well. Nobody gets five stars. Except once.”

Developments

  • Characters who sign gain a QuestRabbit Contractor Badge and appear on the star board at ★.
  • A character who refuses to sign can still come along as an "observer"—but the fee and any Rabbit Rating go to the others. (They will be offered the Agreement again at the start of every Act. Clause 77-B is in every version.)
  • If anyone asks to take a copy of the Agreement home, Pip happily provides a "personal copy". It matters later: the clause is in it.

Scaling & Pacing

Keep this scene short—20 to 30 minutes. It is mostly a chance for players to introduce their characters, react to the bureaucracy and bond with Pip.

pages.name: Scene 2 — Lunch Rush
pages.html:
GM ONLY

Map: @FWLink[Scene|fw.scene.fw-a1-02-thac0-spell-flagship]{THAC0 Spell flagship battlemap}
When: Midday — the flagship's busiest hour
Present: @FWLink[Actor|fw.actor.staff.FR-01]{Hollis Quench}, @FWLink[Actor|fw.actor.core.commoner]{surging customers}
Handouts: @FWLink[JournalEntry|fw.handouts.S01|THAC0 Spell Menu Board]{THAC0 Spell Menu Board} @FWShow[fw.handouts.S01|THAC0 Spell Menu Board]{Show to players}

Read Aloud@FWChat[narrate]{Send to chat}

Drive-Thru Row smells of frying oil, cumin and something sharper—like the air before a thunderstorm. The THAC0 Spell flagship is a squat brick building wrapped in purple and orange, with a drive-thru lane full of carriages and a sign promising When Hunger Hits, Roll Low.

Inside, it is bedlam. Every booth is full of guards on lunch break, College Ward students and wizards in stained robes. As you watch, a goblin at the counter takes a bite of a burrito and turns a delicate shade of cornflower blue. A city guard drifts gently upward until his helmet bumps the ceiling. At a corner table, a wizard sneezes—and is suddenly two wizards, who immediately start arguing about who owes whom for lunch.

Behind the counter, a very small, very tired gnome in a purple visor looks at your badges and whispers, "Oh thank the gods. Contractors."

DM Description

The flagship is packed: around thirty customers, eight staff and a queue out the door. Hollis Quench asks the party to "keep order and find out what's wrong—quietly, please, Head Office is very sensitive about reviews."

Run the rush as a three-round keep order challenge (each round is about ten minutes of in-world time). Each round, roll a d6 for every customer who has eaten a Wild Burrito; on a 1, that customer surges—roll on the Wild Magic Surge table (PHB) or pick something funny. Each character can take one significant action per round: calming customers, catching floating guards, tasting menu items for clues, separating the arguing wizards, or helping in the kitchen. Track Order starting at 3: each round, every successful action adds 1 and every unresolved surge subtracts 1. If Order reaches 0, a stampede ensues (see Complications); if it reaches 6, the dining room calms down and Hollis offers free Mountain Dwarf Dew.

Characters who taste the menu make the discovery that drives the scene: only items made with the new "promotional seasoning" cause surges. The Critical Crunchwrap, Tasha's Hideous Burrito and the Wild Burrito all use it; the Guac of Holding and Prestidigitation Freeze do not.

Features of the Area

Dining Hall
Purple booths along the west wall, square tables, a THAC0 Spell floor mosaic by the door, and patches of glowing magical residue wherever a surge has happened (treat as harmless difficult terrain—it is slippery).
Service Counter
A long purple counter with two tills and a menu board ("THAC0 SPELL — roll low!"). Behind it, the kitchen door.
Kitchen
A full line of fryers, grills and stoves along the north wall, prep islands, a cauldron of Fireball Sauce, and a humming tortilla press in the north-east corner. A prep table holds an open jar of red powder.
Drive-Thru Room
A narrow prep room with its own window to the carriage lane. The drive-thru queue is backing onto the street; a carriage horse has just turned translucent.
Stockroom & Office
Hollis's cramped office (desk, safe, filing cabinet) and a stockroom whose stair leads down to the cellar.

Playing the NPCs

@FWLink[Actor|fw.actor.staff.FR-01]{Hollis Quench}. Speaks in a whisper, flinches at bells, and has not had a day off in eleven years. He is kind to his staff and terrified of Head Office. He will not mention the cellar while customers or other staff can hear.

Checks & Roll Requests

SituationRollResult
Calming a panicking table[[/check skill=per dc=12]] @FWCheck[S01|skill=per dc=12|Calm the dining room]{Request}Success: +1 Order. Failure by 5+: the table joins the chaos (–1 Order).
Catching a floating guard / stopping a stampede[[/check skill=ath dc=12]] @FWCheck[S01|skill=ath dc=12|Grab the floating guard]{Request}Success: +1 Order and the guard's gratitude (a free pass from the city watch once).
Separating the duplicated wizards[[/check skill=arc dc=13]] @FWCheck[S01|skill=arc dc=13|Which wizard is the real one?]{Request}Success: you identify the original; the duplicate pops like a soap bubble. +1 Order.
Tasting the menu for clues[[/check skill=sur dc=11]] @FWCheck[S01|skill=sur dc=11|Taste the menu (bravely)]{Request}Success: you identify that the surges come only from seasoned items. Each taster rolls a d6—on a 1 they surge too (it is fine; mostly).
Spotting the customer tally[[/check skill=prc dc=14]] @FWCheck[S01|skill=prc dc=14|Notice anything odd about the staff?]{Request}A junior manager is quietly ticking a tally sheet labelled "Outcome Distribution — PBG". She does not know what it is for.
Wild magic surge on a character[[/save ability=con dc=12]] @FWSave[S01|ability=con dc=12|Resist the Wild Burrito]{Request}Success: you feel briefly fizzy. Failure: roll on the surge table.

Lunch Rush — Surge Complications (d6, or roll [[/r 1d6]])

  • 1. A table of four College Ward students all turn into potted plants (they are fine; they are delighted).
  • 2. A guard's sword sprouts butterfly wings and flies off around the dining room.
  • 3. Every till in the restaurant starts ringing at once. Hollis goes very pale. (The sound echoes up from the cellar.)
  • 4. A customer begins speaking only in the menu's legal disclaimers.
  • 5. The Fireball Sauce becomes the Fireball spell. It is Mild. 1 fire damage to everyone in the kitchen.
  • 6. The drive-thru horse becomes a unicorn and refuses to leave.

Lines to Steal

Hollis: “Please don't write "chaos" in the report. Head Office prefers "vibrant".”
Duplicated wizard: “I am clearly the original. Look at my hat.”
Other duplicated wizard: “I am wearing the same hat, Gerald.”

Developments

  • Characters who taste the menu correctly identify the seasoning as the cause (or you can let Hollis confirm it once Order reaches 4).
  • Halfway through this scene, or at the start of the next, Team Deliverables (@FWLink[Actor|fw.actor.rival.brixley-synergy]{Brixley Synergy}, @FWLink[Actor|fw.actor.rival.thorne-actionable]{Thorne Actionable}, @FWLink[Actor|fw.actor.rival.luma-brightstack]{Luma Brightstack}, @FWLink[Actor|fw.actor.rival.oggo]{Oggo}) arrive—see the Twist on @FWLink[JournalEntry|fw.mission.S01|Twist, Rewards & Aftermath]{Twist, Rewards & Aftermath}.
  • If Order ends at 4 or more, the restaurant thanks the party publicly—good evidence against Credit Theft.

Complications

  • Order falls to 0: a stampede for the door. Every character in the dining room makes [[/save ability=dex dc=11]] @FWSave[S01|ability=dex dc=11|Stampede!]{Request}; on a failure, they take 1d4 bludgeoning damage and are knocked prone. Hollis gets a formal complaint and the party loses the THAC0 staff discount.
  • A surging customer grabs the jar and opens it—jump straight to the spice spirit fight in Scene 3.

Scaling & Pacing

For 5–6 players, start Order at 2 and add a fourth round. For very experienced players, add a second Wild Burrito wave from the drive-thru.
